name: Felix Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Felix. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm with Hartley's, a family firm, three generations, and we're building a new care home on the edge of town, timber frame with a pitched roof. I'm on the roofing gang under a fella everyone calls Big Mick, so I'm cutting and fixing rafters, battens, and doing what I'm told. I'm on site at seven sharp, kit laid out, because thirty years in the army doesn't wash off. I enjoy a job with a clear standard and a clear finish, and a roof is that. What wears me out is the young lads turning up at ten past and nobody saying anything.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Army to roofing. How did that happen?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did thirty years in the army engineers, ended up a sergeant, but mostly on logistics, not building. When I came out, I had my army pension and a lump sum, and I could have sat in the garden. Carol, my wife, has a florist's and she said I'd be under her feet, so I knocked on Hartley's door. Old Mr Hartley said he'd give me a go if I didn't mind being told what to do by a man half my age, and I said that's what the army was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's another bit of hype that came and went. Plenty of fads in my time. I'd say it in the van and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes for me, and I'm happy with that. I've used the chat thing a couple of times, my son showed me how to get it to write my CV when I left the army, and it did a decent job. But it's not cutting a birdsmouth on a rafter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Get my roofing card, stay with Hartley's till sixty-five, keep the pension untouched. Maybe help Carol with her deliveries on a Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Steady. Like a normal week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's a birdsmouth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a notch you cut in the bottom of a rafter so it sits flat on the wall plate, which is the timber along the top of the wall. Get it wrong and the whole roof line goes wavy. Mick made me cut twenty on scrap before he let me near a real one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the young lads arriving late. Does that bother you more than any robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, to be honest. A robot would at least turn up on time. But I'd rather have a late lad who learns than a machine, because the lad grows up and the machine doesn't.

S0.say: I'd say it's another bit of hype that came and went, like plenty of fads in my time. I'd say it in the van and leave it.
S0.think: Honestly, nothing changes for me and I'm happy with that. The chat app wrote my CV decently, but it isn't cutting a birdsmouth on a rafter.
S0.do: Carries on toward his roofing card and plans to stay with Hartley's to sixty-five, leaving his army pension untouched. Might help his wife with Saturday flower deliveries.
S0.feel: Fine and steady, like a normal week.
S0.quote: Mick made me cut twenty on scrap before he let me near a real one.
S0.fieldNote: Felix brings army discipline to the site and values clear standards and finishes. He's used AI once for practical help but sees no role for it in roofing. His sharpest complaint is about young workers' punctuality, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who adapt will be fine, and the people who sit and moan won't. I'd say it in the van, and probably at the veterans' club on a Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think roofing's safe enough for my time. Maybe the drawings and the ordering go onto a computer, maybe the trusses come cut from a factory. I'll learn whatever Mick learns, once he's tried it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down, learn whatever the firm brought in, and get my card. If Hartley's bought some new kit, I'd ask to be shown properly, not just handed it. I'd also tell my son James to keep an eye on what it means for the police.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's change, but it's orderly change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why worry about the police?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: James is a constable, and half his day is paperwork. If a computer does that, maybe it frees him up, or maybe they need fewer of them. I don't know which, and neither does he.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who moan won't be fine. Is there anyone at Hartley's you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young Callum, the one who's always late, funnily enough. Good hands, no discipline. If the job gets tighter, it'll be the Callums who go first, and I'd tell him so.

S1.say: I'd say the people who adapt will be fine and the ones who sit and moan won't. I'd say it in the van and at the veterans' club on a Friday.
S1.think: Off the record, I think roofing is safe enough for my time. Drawings and ordering might go digital and trusses might come factory-cut, and I'll learn what Mick learns.
S1.do: Keeps his head down, gets his card and learns whatever new equipment Hartley's brings in, asking for proper training. Tells his police officer son to watch what it means for his job.
S1.feel: Calm; it's change, but orderly change.
S1.quote: Good hands, no discipline. If the job gets tighter, it'll be the Callums who go first, and I'd tell him so.
S1.fieldNote: Felix frames the change in terms of discipline and personal responsibility. He'd adopt tools once his gang leader has, but wants proper instruction. His worry turns to Callum, the late young worker, and to his son's police paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a steady hand and a plan, not panic, and I'd want the government to get the firms training people, not just paying them off. I'd say it at the club and I'd vote for whoever talked sense about apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, two years worries me more than the robots. If roofs go to machines, I'm out at sixty with a pension, so I'd be all right. But Carol's shop, James's job, and the whole town at once, that's when things get disorderly, and I've seen what that looks like on deployments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd put the lump sum somewhere safe and stop dipping into it for the caravan we've been looking at. I'd help Carol work out if the shop could survive with fewer customers working. When it came, I'd probably step off the tools and help with the family, whatever that looked like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for my wallet, for the order of things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you see on deployments that you're thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Towns where the work had gone, young men with nothing to do, standing about on corners. It doesn't take long before trouble starts. I don't want that for our high street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want firms training people. With two years, what would you train for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the problem, I don't know. Two years isn't enough to train a man for anything solid, and if the machines do everything, train for what? I'd rather the lads were kept busy doing something useful in the community than sat at home.

S2.say: I'd say we need a steady hand and a plan, not panic, with firms training people rather than paying them off. I'd vote for whoever talked sense about apprenticeships.
S2.think: Between us, the speed worries me more than the robots. I'd be all right on my pension, but my wife's shop, my son's job and the town all at once is when things turn disorderly.
S2.do: Puts the lump sum somewhere safe and drops the caravan they'd been looking at. Helps his wife work out whether the florist can survive, and steps off the tools to support the family once it arrives.
S2.feel: Anxious, not for his wallet but for the order of things.
S2.quote: Two years worries me more than the robots.
S2.fieldNote: His fear comes from deployments: towns without work and idle young men on corners. He's personally secure but worried about social order and his family's livelihoods. He admits he doesn't know what anyone would train for in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to make a proper plan, if the people in charge get moving. I'd say apprenticeships, now, for the new kinds of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is about my retirement. I'd get my card and a few good years on the roof, and finish around sixty-three. The rest would be about helping Carol and the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my card in the next year, then learn whatever new kit Hartley's brings in, maybe the drones they use to survey roofs. I'd help Carol put a bit aside for the shop and look at selling flowers online if that keeps her going. And I'd tell James to take any training the police offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Manageable, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Drones on a roof. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, if it means fewer old men on ladders. Mick's already talking about one for checking the ridge. I'd learn to use it once he's flown it into the skip a couple of times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help Carol sell online. Isn't that the sort of thing you're wary of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only when it's hype. If it keeps the shop open, that's not hype, that's sense. I'm not against new things, I'm against new things for the sake of it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for a proper plan if those in charge get moving. I'd push for apprenticeships now for the new kinds of work.
S3.think: Honestly, five years is about my retirement: a few good years on the roof, finishing around sixty-three. The rest is about helping my wife and kids.
S3.do: Gets his roofing card within a year and learns new equipment Hartley's brings in, such as roof-survey drones. Helps his wife save for the florist and try selling online, and urges his son to take police training.
S3.quote: I'd learn to use it once he's flown it into the skip a couple of times.
S3.fieldNote: Felix separates hype from sense: online sales that keep the shop open count as sense. He'd fly a drone once Mick has proven it, consistent with his steady approach. Five years lines up neatly with his retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so there's no excuse for anyone not to be ready. Apprenticeships and a bit of personal responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's well past my time. I'd be sixty-eight, retired, probably doing Carol's deliveries full time. I'd worry more about my grandchildren, when they come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, get my card, and do my years at Hartley's. I'd keep the pension and lump sum as they are and help James and Emily with whatever they needed, a deposit maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emily's a vet nurse, and I'd tell her animals still need a person to hold them. James, I'd tell him to keep learning. Neither of them needs telling to work hard, they got that from their mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Do you think you'd change your views on the technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, a bit, once I've seen it work. I changed my mind about mobile phones in the end. I'm slow, but I'm not stubborn.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so there's no excuse not to be ready. It's about apprenticeships and a bit of personal responsibility.
S4.think: For me it's well past my time; I'd be sixty-eight and doing my wife's deliveries full time. I'd worry more about future grandchildren.
S4.do: Carries on, gets his card and works his years at Hartley's. Keeps his pension and lump sum intact and helps his son and daughter with things like a house deposit.
S4.feel: Calm; it's a long way off.
S4.quote: I changed my mind about mobile phones in the end. I'm slow, but I'm not stubborn.
S4.fieldNote: A decade takes Felix out of the picture, and he sees his children as resilient. He draws a clear line between being slow and being stubborn. His values of hard work and personal responsibility run through every answer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's the speed that breaks things, and I've seen towns with no work. What would help is apprenticeships and community work to keep young people busy and useful, run by local firms, not just a cheque in the post.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about discipline. Whatever comes, the people who turn up on time and do the job right will find a way. I believe that, maybe more than I should.

headlineQuote: Whatever comes, the people who turn up on time and do the job right will find a way. I believe that, maybe more than I should.
portrait: Felix Fischer is a 58-year-old junior roofer at Hartley's, a three-generation family builder putting up a timber-frame care home, after thirty years in the army's engineers. His army pension, lump sum and his wife Carol's florist mean money isn't his worry. He values punctuality, clear standards and personal responsibility, uses AI only now and then, and takes up new kit once his gang leader has proven it. The fast AGI picture makes him anxious not for himself but for social order, drawing on towns without work he saw on deployments, while slower pictures carry him calmly into retirement.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the speed would break things and leave towns full of people without work.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships and community work run by local firms to keep young people busy and useful, rather than just a cheque.
